message.reasoning:
I'm looking at this large ObjectMapper class and need to write a JUnit 4 test suite maximizing branch coverage using real Jackson databind — but I notice the classpath only lists jackson-core and jackson-annotations, missing the actual jackson-databind jar needed for ObjectMapper itself. I need to figure out how to handle this dependency gap.

Then I realize this makes sense: ObjectMapper is the source code under test (SUT), compiled locally as part of the project being built, similar to a Defects4J setup, so it doesn't need to appear as a separate jar dependency — only its supporting classes within the same package need to be present. This means I can write tests using ObjectMapper normally, covering constructors, readValue, writeValueAsString, treeToValue, valueToTree, configure, enable/disable, and registerModule, starting with constructor variations.

Beyond that, I'm planning coverage for version(), module registration edge cases like null names/versions and duplicate registration handling, batch module registration methods, module discovery, mix-in configuration, visibility checkers, subtype resolution, annotation introspectors, property naming strategies, serialization inclusion settings, and default pretty printer configuration.

I'll also need tests for default typing behavior—checking that EXTERNAL_PROPERTY throws an exception, verifying enable/disable/set variants, and exercising DefaultTypeResolverBuilder.useForType() across different DefaultTyping enum values and JavaType scenarios like arrays, concrete types, Object, final types, and TreeNode subtypes. Beyond that there's type factory and node factory configuration, problem handler management, config setters for serialization/deserialization, filter providers, base64 variant settings, factory getters, and date format configuration.

Continuing through this list: handler instantiator, injectable values, locale, timezone settings, then feature enable/disable/configure checks across MapperFeature, SerializationFeature, DeserializationFeature, JsonParser.Feature, JsonGenerator.Feature, and JsonFactory.Feature. I also need coverage for readValue with different parser/type combinations, readTree behavior across null tokens and various input sources, readValues variants, and writeValue/writeTree tests including indented output and closeable handling.

I'm continuing to map out remaining coverage: tree creation helpers, treeAsTokens, treeToValue with its cast shortcut and exception wrapping, valueToTree null vs normal handling, canSerialize/canDeserialize checks, the various readValue/writeValue overloads across files and streams, writer()/reader() variant methods, convertValue behavior for null and cast shortcuts, and finally acceptJsonFormatVisitor's null-argument exception cases.

Given how extensive this list is, I'm deciding to scope the test class down to roughly 60-80 methods covering the major branches rather than every single overload, using a simple POJO with basic fields and getters/setters as the test fixture, plus a mock Module implementation for testing registerModule since Module is abstract with methods like getModuleName, version, and setupModule that need overriding.

I'm working through the edge cases for registerModule: null module name throws IllegalArgumentException, null version also throws but only checked after the name check passes, and getTypeId defaults to null unless overridden for typeId-based tests. I also need to exercise SetupContext methods like addSerializers and addDeserializers within the module's setup logic.

Given the sheer breadth of SetupContext methods, I don't think each one needs deep individual coverage since most just delegate to already-tested mapper functionality—invoking each once through a test module should be sufficient for branch coverage, given the scope constraints I'm working under.

I'm planning around 60 test methods targeting the most fault-prone branches, then moving into writing actual test code, starting with a simple POJO bean with name/value fields plus a Closeable bean to verify resource-closing behavior during serialization.

For DefaultTypeResolverBuilder, I'm setting up test cases using different JavaType instances (Object, String, Number) to exercise useForType's branching logic across concrete, final, and abstract types.

I need more type variety: primitive arrays, ArrayList, and TreeNode subtypes like JsonNode/ObjectNode, since the code has special-case handling excluding TreeNode types from being treated as non-concrete for certain typing modes.

Now I'm tracing through the test scenarios for each typing setting - checking Object vs String vs Number for JAVA_LANG_OBJECT and OBJECT_AND_NON_CONCRETE modes, and confirming JsonNode gets excluded despite being non-concrete since it's a TreeNode. Then verifying array types get their element type peeled off for the NON_CONCRETE_AND_ARRAYS check.

String and Boolean are excluded via the isFinal check, so testing ArrayList.class (non-final, concrete) should give true, String[].class should peel to String and give false, and JsonNode.class should give false since it's TreeNode-assignable despite not being final.

Now I'm sketching out test module classes that override getModuleName and version using Jackson's Version.unknownVersion(), plus variants for testing typeId overrides and missing module names.

For registerModule, I'm planning tests covering null module name throwing an error, null version throwing an error, normal registration calling setupModule (verified via a flag), and duplicate registration behavior tied to the IGNORE_DUPLICATE_MODULE_REGISTRATIONS feature, though I'll explicitly toggle that flag since I'm not fully certain of its default value.

I also want to cover registerModules with varargs and Iterable, plus findModules/findModules(ClassLoader) and findAndRegisterModules which should delegate to registerModules(findModules()).

For mix-ins, I'll test addMixIn plus findMixInClassFor and mixInCount, setMixIns with a map, and setMixInResolver to confirm custom resolvers supply mappings when no local mapping exists.

For visibility, I need to check getVisibilityChecker isn't null, verify setVisibility(VisibilityChecker) properly updates the serialization config, and confirm setVisibility(PropertyAccessor.FIELD, Visibility.ANY) enables field-based serialization by checking output includes private field names. For subtype resolution I'll test getSubtypeResolver, setSubtypeResolver with a new StdSubtypeResolver, and registerSubtypes for both Class and NamedType variants. For annotation introspectors I'll verify setAnnotationIntrospector and setAnnotationIntrospectors don't throw and accept multiple introspectors.

For property naming, I'll test that setPropertyNamingStrategy(SNAKE_CASE) converts camelCase getters into snake_case JSON keys. For serialization inclusion, I'll confirm NON_NULL excludes null fields from output. For pretty printing, I'll test that a custom default pretty printer gets used when indentation is enabled and no generator-level printer is set. For default typing, I'm considering how to verify type metadata gets embedded when serializing an Object-typed field -- possibly by round-tripping a List<Object> through serialization and deserialization to confirm the original type is preserved, though this approach feels overly complex and I may need a simpler check.

A cleaner test: enable default typing and serialize a bean assigned to an Object-typed field, then assert the JSON contains the class name string, confirming type info is embedded since Object-declared values qualify for typing. I should also test enableDefaultTyping with specific strategies like OBJECT_AND_NON_CONCRETE paired with As.PROPERTY, and verify that using As.EXTERNAL_PROPERTY throws an IllegalArgumentException.

I also want to cover enableDefaultTypingAsProperty with a custom property name, and confirm disableDefaultTyping (or setting null) removes the type metadata after a prior enable call. For TypeFactory and NodeFactory, I'll verify getters return non-null defaults, that setters chain properly, and that constructType resolves the right JavaType. I should also test adding and clearing problem handlers to confirm unknown properties don't throw when a custom handler is registered, and test setConfig for both deserialization and serialization configs by modifying an existing config via with() and reapplying it.

For the remaining odds and ends I want to test filter providers affecting serialized output, custom Base64 variants when serializing byte arrays, verifying getFactory returns the same JsonFactory instance, custom DateFormat affecting Date field serialization, HandlerInstantiator's oddly-typed setter still returning a valid mapper, and InjectableValues round-tripping through getters and setters.

I also plan to cover Locale/TimeZone setters, then systematically walk through MapperFeature, SerializationFeature, DeserializationFeature, JsonParser.Feature, and JsonGenerator.Feature -- checking default enabled states, single configure calls, and both the single-arg and varargs forms of enable/disable. Finally I want to test reading values and trees directly through a JsonParser instance, including checking behavior before any token has been read.

Now I'm mapping out edge cases for readTree: handling empty input (which should return null after nextToken returns null), and parsing a bare "null" literal into a NullNode. I also want to test readValues for streaming multiple values off an unwrapped sequence, and cover the various readTree overloads across different input sources like strings, streams, files, and URLs.

For empty string input specifically, I need to trace through whether readTree(String) throws a JsonMappingException for "No content to map" versus returning null, since it routes through _readMapAndClose and _initForReading rather than the direct JsonParser path.

I'll skip worrying about that edge case and instead focus on testing the normal use case plus verifying that an empty string throws a JsonMappingException, since readTree(String) doesn't handle EOF the way readTree(JsonParser) does -- this covers the throw branch nicely. I'll test readTree(byte[]) the same way.

Then I'll test readTree(File) using a temp file with JSON content, and readTree(Reader) with a StringReader, possibly skipping readTree(URL) unless I convert a temp file's URI to a URL. For writeValue(JsonGenerator, Object), I'll cover the normal path without a Closeable and without INDENT_OUTPUT, then test with INDENT_OUTPUT enabled where the generator lacks a pretty printer to hit that branch.

I also need to test INDENT_OUTPUT enabled with a generator whose pretty printer is already set to hit the false branch of that inner check, plus CLOSE_CLOSEABLE enabled with a Closeable value to verify it's closed via _writeCloseableValue, and CLOSE_CLOSEABLE disabled or non-Closeable values with FLUSH_AFTER_WRITE_VALUE toggled both ways. Then writeTree(JsonGenerator, TreeNode/JsonNode), createObjectNode/createArrayNode, and treeAsTokens are straightforward round-trip tests, and treeToValue needs a case testing the cast shortcut when the node is an ObjectNode matching the target value type.

For treeToValue I want to verify the shortcut returns the exact same instance when valueType is assignable and not Object.class, contrast that with the normal path where valueType is a bean class requiring full deserialization through readValue, and also check that explicitly passing Object.class forces the full path even though it'd otherwise qualify for the shortcut -- likely deserializing into a LinkedHashMap. I'm noting that testing the wrapped IOException-to-IllegalArgumentException case is tricky without mocking real I/O failures, so I may skip or flag it as uncertain.

For valueToTree, I'm checking that a null input returns null and that a normal bean produces the expected ObjectNode fields. For canSerialize, I plan to test a straightforward serializable case like String.class or SimpleBean.class returning true, and consider whether a false case is feasible to construct without complex setup -- deciding it's simpler to focus on the true case for now.

For canSerialize with an AtomicReference, I want to confirm the reference stays null in the success case since no exception is thrown, verified with an AtomicReference<Throwable>. For canDeserialize, I'm considering testing SimpleBean as a true case, and exploring whether an interface like List.class would resolve deserialization through a default implementation like ArrayList, while looking for a class that isn't instantiable to produce a false case.

I'm testing an abstract class with no registered implementation and no default typing to confirm canDeserialize returns false, and checking the AtomicReference<Throwable> captures a non-null cause in that scenario. For the extended readValue methods, I'm planning coverage of the main variants -- String, TypeReference, JavaType, byte array, offset/length byte array, InputStream, Reader, File, and URL -- using a temp file for the file and URL cases, and similarly outlining writeValue tests for File and OutputStream targets.

I'm now planning tests for writer() and reader() variants -- covering writeValue(Writer,...), writeValueAsString, writeValueAsBytes with roundtrip verification via readValue, then a representative subset of writer() overloads (SerializationFeature, DateFormat, writerWithView, writerFor, PrettyPrinter, FilterProvider, FormatSchema with an incompatible schema expecting IllegalArgumentException, Base64Variant, CharacterEscapes, ContextAttributes, and the deprecated writerWithType methods), followed by the analogous reader() overloads including readerForUpdating.

For convertValue, I'm testing null input returns null, a same-type String shortcut returns the identical instance via identity check, targetType Object.class skips the shortcut and goes through full serialize/deserialize producing a Map, and generic target types like List<String> via TypeReference correctly skip the shortcut even when assignable.

Now I'm checking acceptJsonFormatVisitor with a null Class argument -- tracing whether constructType(null) throws before the null-check in the JavaType overload even gets reached, since TypeFactory might raise an IllegalArgumentException for null type rather than hitting my intended null check path.

For the Class<?> overload, I'll test with a valid type (SimpleBean.class) and use Mockito to mock the JsonFormatVisitorWrapper interface, avoiding manual no-op implementation of all its methods.

I should also verify _verifySchemaType behavior with writer(FormatSchema) and reader(FormatSchema), checking that null schemas don't throw.

Since JsonFactory's default canUseSchema always returns false for non-CSV factories, passing any non-null FormatSchema mock to a plain ObjectMapper's writer/reader should throw an IllegalArgumentException, so I can test that with a mocked FormatSchema.

I also want to exercise the exception path inside _configAndWriteValue, where a failure during serialization triggers the AUTO_CLOSE_JSON_CONTENT-disabled cleanup branch in the finally block -- I can trigger this by serializing an object whose getter throws or that otherwise causes a JsonMappingException.

Simplest bet: use an empty bean with no visible properties and FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS enabled, since writeValue on such an object should throw a JsonMappingException about no serializer being found.

Now I'm sketching a test for MappingIterator.readValues, setting up a parser over a stream of simple integers.

I'll skip the manual advance and trust MappingIterator to handle it, following the common Jackson usage pattern. For the readValues overloads taking TypeReference and ResolvedType, I'll just add one test call each for coverage.

Since JavaType implements ResolvedType, I can use mapper.constructType(SimpleBean.class) directly as the ResolvedType argument, covering that overload uniquely. Now I'm assembling the final test file, setting up the ObjectMapper in @Before and adding a TemporaryFolder rule for file/URL-based tests, plus the necessary Module, Version, and SetupContext imports.

Compiling the full list of imports I'll need: PropertyNamingStrategy, JsonInclude.Include, Base64Variants, VisibilityChecker, PropertyAccessor, JsonAutoDetect.Visibility, NamedType, StdSubtypeResolver, JsonNodeFactory, TreeNode, DeserializationProblemHandler, and InjectableValues, all from their respective Jackson packages.

I also need SimpleFilterProvider for testing setFilterProvider, though I'll keep that test shallow -- just verifying the chain returns the mapper without exceptions rather than deep-testing actual filtering behavior. For FormatSchema and JsonFormatVisitorWrapper, I'll use Mockito mocks since these are typically implemented by consumers, and I'll need CharacterEscapes as well.

Since CharacterEscapes is abstract, I'm creating an anonymous subclass implementing the two required methods, one returning the standard ASCII escape codes and the other returning null for the escape sequence. For ContextAttributes I can just use the empty instance, and for HandlerInstantiator I'll likely just pass null since the setter itself has no branching logic to exercise.

I confirm PropertyNamingStrategy.SNAKE_CASE is a valid static field, then move to setting up Module tests, importing Module, SetupContext, and Version so I can define static nested test module classes extending the abstract Module class with name, version, and type ID fields along with a flag tracking whether setup was called.

I'm planning test cases: registering a module with a null name should throw an IllegalArgumentException, one with a null version, and a normal successful registration case.

For duplicate handling, I'm testing that with IGNORE_DUPLICATE_MODULE_REGISTRATIONS enabled, registering a module twice with the same typeId only calls setup once, and I'm setting up a second module instance sharing that typeId to verify the skip behavior.

Then I check the opposite case where the feature is disabled so both calls to setupModule fire, followed by tests for registering multiple modules via array and iterable, and basic sanity checks for findModules and findAndRegisterModules. Next I'm moving on to writing tests for DefaultTypeResolverBuilder.

I want to keep the test suite comprehensive but manageable, aiming for around 70 methods total, and since I can't actually execute the code, I need to rely on my knowledge of this specific Jackson version's behavior, flagging uncertain assumptions with comments where needed. I'm double-checking the default value for the IGNORE_DUPLICATE_MODULE_REGISTRATIONS feature before finalizing these tests.

I'll explicitly set feature flags rather than relying on defaults to keep tests deterministic, then move on to writing the SimpleBean, EmptyBean, CloseableBean, and AbstractNoImpl helper classes. I'm also confirming exception hierarchy details for JsonMappingException so I can use `@Test(expected=...)` correctly, and checking how `canDeserialize` behaves with abstract classes lacking default constructors.

I'll note that `canDeserialize` for an abstract class without registered subtypes likely returns false since Jackson can't find an implementation via AbstractTypeResolver, so I'll write that test case with a comment flagging it's based on typical Jackson behavior rather than certainty. For interfaces like `List.class`, though, canDeserialize should return true since Jackson defaults to ArrayList via CollectionDeserializer.

Given the effort constraints, I'll finalize the code now, adding comments where assumptions are uncertain -- covering things like EXTERNAL_PROPERTY throwing an exception with default typing enabled, and working through how `useForType` handles arrays of non-concrete types like `JsonNode[].class` by checking whether the content type is abstract and falls into the OBJECT_AND_NON_CONCRETE branch.

I'm tracing through how the NON_FINAL case behaves for both array and non-array types, checking finality and TreeNode assignability to confirm the logic matches expectations for cases like `Number.class`.

For JAVA_LANG_OBJECT and OBJECT_AND_NON_CONCRETE, I'm verifying the short-circuit behavior: `Object.class` always returns true regardless of concreteness, while concrete non-Object classes like `ArrayList.class` return false. With the test matrix confirmed, I'm ready to write the actual test code.

I'm ensuring SimpleBean has a default no-arg constructor plus getters/setters so Jackson can round-trip it without custom creators. For the writer(FormatSchema) test, I recall the base JsonFactory.canUseSchema always returns false unless overridden by format-specific factories (CBOR, CSV, etc.), so passing a mocked non-null FormatSchema to a default ObjectMapper's writer(schema) should trigger an IllegalArgumentException.

I want to test that null schema passed to writer/reader is safely skipped without throwing, and confirm the protected schema-verification logic is fully exercised through those paths already. For acceptJsonFormatVisitor, I'm cautious about testing a null Class argument since constructType's behavior with null Type is unclear, so I'll stick to testing the null JavaType overload where the error message is more predictable.

I'll also add a test confirming a valid Class overload runs successfully using a mocked visitor, relying on Mockito's default null returns from unstubbed interface methods -- assuming the serializer tolerates nulls, which is typical for BeanSerializer. With that settled, I'm ready to finalize the test code.

Simplest approach is placing the test class directly in the `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind` package to avoid needing separate imports for most referenced classes, since many of them already live there.

Actually, to satisfy the explicit import requirement, I'll place the test in a separate package instead, like a testsuite subpackage, and import ObjectMapper directly from its actual location.

Actually I'll skip the package declaration entirely and just use imports, since default package classes can still reference public members from named packages fine, and I've confirmed only public API is needed. Let me finalize the file this way.

Now I'm planning the imports needed—TemporaryFolder from JUnit rules, StringWriter, ByteArrayOutputStream, File, and various java.util classes—plus the nested test classes like an "EmptyBean" with zero properties to trigger the FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS exception path. Time to write out the full test code.

I also want to cover the root-wrapping branch, so I'll add a `RootBean` annotated with `@JsonRootName("root")` and test that serializing with `WRAP_ROOT_VALUE` and deserializing with `UNWRAP_ROOT_VALUE` correctly round-trips through the wrapped structure.

I should also test the failure branches inside `_unwrapAndDeserialize`: a mismatched root name should throw a `JsonMappingException`, a missing `START_OBJECT` wrapper should throw a different exception, and an empty object (where `nextToken` returns `END_OBJECT` instead of `FIELD_NAME`) should trigger the "Current token not FIELD_NAME" branch. I'll skip the END_OBJECT mismatch case since it's hard to trigger without deliberately corrupting the input.

I'm uncertain about the exact package for `@JsonRootName` since it moved between `jackson-databind` and `jackson-annotations` across versions, so to avoid compatibility issues I'll just rely on the default root name behavior for unannotated classes rather than using the annotation directly.

For SimpleBean, enabling `WRAP_ROOT_VALUE` should produce serialized JSON with the class's simple name as the wrapping key, giving something like `{"SimpleBean":{"name":...,"value":...}}`.

Then I need to test unwrapping: enabling `UNWRAP_ROOT_VALUE` and calling `readValue` should correctly strip that wrapper back into a SimpleBean. I also want to verify error handling - if I craft JSON with a mismatched wrapper name like `"WrongName"` instead of `"SimpleBean"`, deserialization with UNWRAP_ROOT_VALUE enabled should throw a JsonMappingException due to the name mismatch. Similarly, if the JSON content isn't an object at all (e.g., just a plain string), the parser should fail because the first token isn't START_OBJECT as expected.

I'm tracing through the exact code path: when the token isn't VALUE_NULL/END_ARRAY/END_OBJECT, it goes through `_unwrapAndDeserialize`, which checks that the current token is START_OBJECT and throws otherwise. I also want to test an empty object case—`{}`—where after START_OBJECT is confirmed, the next token should be FIELD_NAME but instead gets END_OBJECT, triggering a different exception about the current token not being FIELD_NAME. These three exception scenarios plus one success case with `readValue(String, Class)` and UNWRAP_ROOT_VALUE enabled seem like solid, targeted tests to add.

I also want to cover the deserializer caching in `_findRootDeserializer`—the first call misses the cache and populates it via `ctxt.findRootValueDeserializer`, while a second call for the same type should hit the cache. Since there's no way to directly observe cache hits from outside without instrumentation, I'll just add a test that calls `readValue` twice with the same type and asserts equal results, noting in a comment that this exercises both the cache-miss and cache-hit branches even though the assertion can't distinguish between them.

Given how large the scope already is, I'll finalize now and write representative tests rather than covering every overloaded reader/writer method, noting the remaining overloads follow identical patterns. I'll structure the test class `ObjectMapperTest` in the default package with JUnit and Mockito imports, using `mapper.getFactory().createParser(String)` as a helper for creating parsers, and organize it into sections mirroring the original class for clarity.

I'm also adding a `PrivateFieldBean` with a private field and no getter to test visibility settings—by default it serializes as empty since only public getters/fields are auto-detected, but enabling field visibility should expose the property and avoid triggering FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS.

Assuming @Before creates a fresh mapper each test, that's fine. I also need an abstract class with an unimplemented method to test canDeserialize returning false, using constructType to get its JavaType. Now I'll assemble the full test file, keeping an eye on hitting roughly seventy test methods total.

I should also test the direct constructors: ObjectMapper(JsonFactory), the default ObjectMapper(), and ObjectMapper(JsonFactory, sp, dc), though the latter with non-null serializer/deserializer providers might be too complex to construct given the DefaultSerializerProvider setup.

I want to verify that when a JsonFactory already has a codec set, constructing an ObjectMapper with that factory doesn't overwrite the existing codec, since the code only sets it if the codec is currently null. I'm writing a test that sets a codec on a factory before passing it to the ObjectMapper constructor, then asserts the original codec remains unchanged.

I also realize the needOrder XOR branch involving requiresPropertyOrdering() versus SORT_PROPERTIES_ALPHABETICALLY is hard to trigger with a default JsonFactory since both are false, so hitting the true branch would require a custom JsonFactory subclass overriding requiresPropertyOrdering.

Now I'm ready to write up the final answer with the complete test code and a summary table covering the branches tested.
